newsitem.title: USA: Dow sets record despite weak technology stocks.
newsitem.headline: Dow sets record despite weak technology stocks.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rose modestly Friday to set a record, shrugging off weakness in technology issues as portfolio managers snapped up big, relatively safe stocks before the year-end.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 14.23 points to 6,560.91, topping the previous record of 6,547.79 set on Nov. 25. For the week, the Dow rose 76.51 points.

In the broader market, gainers beat losers 1,495 to 936 on New York Stock Exchange volume of 252.5 million shares -- the quietest full session this year. That distinction had been held by Thursday's session, when 253.4 million shares traded.
Friday's gains extended the Dow's rally to its eighth consecutive session.
Technology stocks came under pressure, however, after software company Computer Associates warned of lower-than-anticipated revenues.

"Computer Associates almost stopped the Santa Claus rally. Technology stocks are coming under some pressure, particularly the software issues," said A.C. Moore, senior investment strategist at Dunvegan Associates.
The technology studded Nasdaq Composite index fell 3.19 to 1,291.38. For the week it gained 2.82 points.

On the NYSE, Computer Associates dropped 13-1/4 to 48-1/2. The company, citing weakness in Europe, forecast revenue for the third quarter ending Dec. 31 at between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, less than the consensus estimate of $1.2 billion. Morgan Stanley and Smith Barney downgraded the stock.
Among other technology shares, Motorola fell 1-1/2 to 61-3/4, Intel fell 1-1/4 to 135-3/8, Microsoft lost 1-1/4 to 84-1/4 and IBM was off 5/8 to 155-1/4.

Stocks received support from stronger bond prices. The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 20/32, or $6.25 per $1,000 face value. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction to the price, fell to 6.54 percent from 6.59 percent Thursday.

Bonds rose on an unexpected 1.6 percent drop in November orders of durable goods. It was the first decline in orders for big-ticket items in three months and stood in contrast with a 0.1 percent rise expected by Wall Street.
In another economic report, jobless claims fell to 335,000 for the week ended Dec. 21, compared with 346,000 expected by private economists.
Outside the technology sector, some interest rate-sensitive issues declined even though bond prices rose.
Wells Fargo lost 1-5/8 to 278-5/8, Citicorp fell 1/4 to 106-3/8 and Bankers Trust slipped 1/4 to 88.
"Otherwise, it's very featureless," Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage, said.

Moore said he expected activity to pick up next week, when November leading indicators, December consumer confidence and the National Association of Purchasing Managers index are scheduled to be released. U.S. financial markets will be closed on Wednesday, New Year's Day.

Among individual issues, Zitel surged 9-1/8 to 61-1/4 amid short-covering and an optimistic outlook for Matridigm Corp., a software company that specialises in the so-called Year 2000 bug. Zitel owns 35 percent of Matridigm.

InVision Technologies surged six to 31-1/2. It won a $52 million FAA contract for its bomb detection devices. The government has the option to buy more systems in the second year which would boost the contract's value to $110.9 million.
TSR Inc. soared 10-1/2 to 37-1/2 after the company said its Year 2000 conversion software, CATCH/21 completed a satisfactory field test.
After the closing bell, Nordstrom warned of an earnings shortfall for the quarter ended Jan. 31 due to lower holiday sales. The stock closed down 1/2 to 37-1/2.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 0.97 to 756.79 -- just shy of its record of 757.03 also set on Nov. 25. The American Stock Exchange index fell 0.90 to 581.93.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,288.857, up 17.941 points, or 0.25 percent.
